pages.text: Taxila is a historic city and World Heritage Site in the Punjab province of Pakistan. Founded around 1000 BC, it is one of the oldest cities in South Asia. Today, it is a popular tourist spot that attracts up to one million visitors every year.

pages.text: The city was historically known as Takṣaśilā in Sanskrit. The region around Taxila was settled by the Neolithic era, with ruins dating to 1000 BCE. Early Harappan period ruins from around 1300 BCE have also been discovered in the area.

pages.text: During his invasion of the Indus Valley, Alexander the Great gained control of Taxila in 326 BCE after its ruler surrendered without a battle. In the following centuries, the Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Indo-Parthians, and Kushans successively made Taxila their capital city.

evidence.articleCaption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

pages.text: Some scholars consider ancient Taxila to be one of the earliest education centres in South Asia. It had great influence on Hindu culture and the Sanskrit language. The strategist Chanakya and the grammarian Pāṇini were both part of the community at Taxila.
pages.caption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

pages.text: In the fifth century, the invading Hunas devastated the city, and it eventually fell into decline. In the mid-nineteenth century, ruins of ancient Taxila were rediscovered by British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham. In 1980, UNESCO designated Taxila as a World Heritage Site.

C1-C2.headline: Urban Evolution and Legacy of Taxila

pages.text: Taxila, historically recognized as Takshaśilā, is situated on the eastern bank of the Indus River in northern Punjab, Pakistan. Archaeological investigations indicate that the region sustained settlement activity from the Neolithic and Early Harappan periods before establishing major urban centers.
pages.caption: Eastern border of the Achaemenid Empire

pages.text: As a pivotal junction between South Asia and Central Asia, the city functioned successively as a provincial capital or imperial seat under the Achaemenid Empire, the Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Indo-Parthians, and Kushans.

pages.text: While certain researchers interpret the traditional educational framework of Taxila as one of the earliest tertiary centers in the region, others note structural differences compared to later institutional universities like Nalanda. Nevertheless, the settlement exerted profound influence on Sanskrit linguistics and classical literature.
pages.caption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

evidence.articleCaption: A view over the ruins of Sirkap.

pages.text: The geopolitical stability of the city deteriorated following fifth-century invasions by the Kidarites and Hephthalite-associated forces, compounded by regional trade disruptions and shifting imperial conflicts. Subsequent centuries saw the site fall into progressive decline and obscurity.
pages.caption: The Dharmarajika Stupa

pages.text: Nineteenth-century rediscovery and subsequent excavations by archaeologists uncovered four distinct urban settlement sites spanning multiple epochs. In recognition of its stratigraphic contribution to South Asian urban evolution, UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980.
